==English== {{wp}} ===Etymology=== {{dercat|en|ett}} From {{inh|en|enm|market}}, from late {{inh|en|ang|market||market}} and {{der|en|xno|markiet}} ({{der|en|fro|marchié}}); all ultimately from {{der|en|la|mercātus||trade, market}}, from {{m|la|mercor||to trade, deal in, buy}}, itself derived from {{m|la|merx||wares, merchandise}}. {{doublet|en|mart}}. Cognate with {{cog|fy|merk||market}}, {{cog|nl|markt}}, {{cog|de|Markt}}, {{cog|da|-}} and {{cog|no|marked||market}}, {{cog|fo|-}} and {{cog|is|markaður||market}}, {{cog|sv|marknad||market}}. Displaced native {{noncog|ang|stapol}}. ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/ˈmɑːkɪt/|a=UK}} ** {{audio|en|En-uk-market.ogg|a=UK}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈmɑɹkɪt/|/ˈmɑɹkət/|a=US}} ** {{audio|en|en-us-market.ogg|a=US}} * {{hyphenation|en|mar|ket}} * {{rhymes|en|ɑː(ɹ)kɪt|ɑː(ɹ)kət|s=2}} ===Noun=== {{en-noun}} # {{senseid|en|gathering of people for trading, often periodic at a set time}} A [[gathering]] of [[people]] for the [[purchase]] and [[sale]] of [[merchandise]], often [[periodic]] at a set [[time]]. #: {{syn|en|mart#Noun|fair}} #: {{ux|en|The right to hold a weekly '''market''' was an invaluable privilege not given to all towns in the Middle Ages.}} #: {{ux|en|There's a '''market''' every Thursday and Saturday in the town square.}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=1949|author=w:Ludwig Von Mises|title=w:Human Action |passage=The '''market''' is a process, actuated by the interplay of the actions of the various individuals cooperating under the division of labor.}} # {{senseid|en|Q132510}}A relatively spacious outdoor or covered site where [[trader]]s set up [[stall]]s, either temporarily or permanently or semi-permanently, and [[buyer]]s [[browse]] the merchandise. #: {{syn|en|marketplace|bazaar|arcade}} #: {{ux|en|This site on North Street used to be the '''market''', until it was redeveloped.}} #* {{RQ:Allingham China Governess|chapter=Foreword|passage=‘I understand that the district was considered a sort of sanctuary,’ the Chief was saying. ‘{{nb...}} They tell me there was a recognized swag '''market''' down here.’}} # {{senseid|en|grocery store, convenience store, or similar store}} Any physical [[store#Noun|store]] selling [[groceries#Noun|groceries]], such as a [[grocery store]] or [[convenience store]]. #: {{hypo|en|supermarket}} #: {{ux|en|Stop by the '''market''' on your way home and pick up some milk.}} #* {{quote-book |en |year=1999 |last=Mendelson |first=Cheryl |authorlink=Cheryl Mendelson |title=Home Comforts: The Art and Science of Keeping House |publisher=Scribner |page=45-46 |isbn=9780684814650 |passage=Mixes [such as cake mixes, pancake mixes, or sauce mixes] are sometimes a reasonable alternative and sometimes not. {{...}} Pancake mixes often offer no advantages at all. Nonetheless, there are times when you would be foolish not to use a mix. Perhaps a domestic emergency occurs. Perhaps cupcakes must be brought to school tomorrow morning, but when you stop at the '''market''' on your way home from work, you cannot remember whether you have baking powder, cream of tartar, baking soda, nutmeg, cake flour, chocolate, or vanilla on your shelf, or you want to go through the “five items or fewer” line. So you buy the mix. Only a glutton for punishment would do otherwise.}} # {{senseid|en|group of potential or current customers}} A [[group]] of [[potential]] or current [[customer]]s for one's [[product]]. #: {{syn|en|sale}} #: {{ux|en|We believe that the '''market''' for the new widget will be the older homeowner.}} #: {{ux|en|Senior citizens are our core '''market''' at present, and we can't afford to alienate them as we explore other markets.}} #* {{RQ:Mill Political Economy |passage=There is a third thing to be considered: how a '''market''' can be created for produce, or how production can be limited to the capacities of the market.}} # {{senseid|en|region where buyers and demand exist}} A [[geographical]] [[area]] or [[region]] where a certain [[commercial]] [[demand]] exists. #: {{ux|en|Foreign '''markets''' were lost as our currency rose versus their valuta.}} # {{senseid|en|particular system for trading in certain goods}} A formally organized, sometimes monopolistic, system of trading in specified goods or effects. #: {{cot|en|distribution channel}} #: {{ux|en|The stock '''market''' ceased to be monopolized by the paper-shuffling national stock exchanges with the advent of Internet '''markets'''.}} #* {{quote-journal|en|year=1980|journal=InfoWorld|volume=2|issue=20 |passage=As they were approaching bankruptcy from being knocked out of the calculator '''market''', they began development on the first commercially available microcomputer, the Altair.}} #* {{RQ:Economist|date=2014-03-15|volume=410|issue=8878 |title=Turn it off|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140316165950/http://www.economist.com/news/leaders/21598997-american-regulators-should-block-comcasts-proposed-deal-time-warner-cable-turn-it|passage=If the takeover is approved, Comcast would control 20 of the top 25 cable '''markets''', {{...}}. {{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[join]] or [[unite]] (e.g. one thing to another, or as several [[particular]]s) so as to increase the number, augment the quantity{{,}} or enlarge the magnitude, or so as to form into one aggregate.

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To append (e.g. a statement); to say further information.

#* {{RQ:Baum Wizard of Oz|chapter=23|passage="Bless your dear heart," she said, "I am sure I can tell you of a way to get back to Kansas." Then she '''added''', "But, if I do, you must give me the Golden Cap."}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To intensify; to augment; to increase.
#: {{ux|en|It '''adds''' to our anxiety.}}
#* {{RQ:KJV|1 Kings|12|14|passage=I will '''add''' to your yoke}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-06-29|volume=407|issue=8842|page=72–3
|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/international/science-and-technology/21580133-how-microbes-promote-liver-cancer-overweight-punch-gut A punch in the gut]
|passage=Mostly, the microbiome is beneficial.{{...}}Research over the past few years, however, has implicated it in diseases from atherosclerosis to asthma to autism. Dr Yoshimoto and his colleagues would like to '''add''' liver cancer to that list.}}

===Etymology===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:cutten|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|cutten}}, of {{der|en|gmq}} origin, from {{der|en|non|*kytja}}, {{m|non|*kutta}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*kutjaną}}, {{m|gem-pro|*kuttaną|t=to cut}}, of uncertain origin, perhaps related to {{der|en|gem-pro|*kwetwą|t=meat, flesh}} (compare {{cog|non|kvett|t=meat}}). Sometimes instead compared to {{cog|fr|couteau}}, itself from {{cog|la|culter|t=knife}}.<ref>{{R:Online_Etymology_Dictionary}}</ref>

Compare {{cog|sco|kut}}, {{m|sco|kit|t=to cut}}); also akin to Middle {{cog|sv|kotta|t=to cut or carve with a knife}} (compare dialectal {{cog|sv|kåta}}, {{m|sv|kuta|t=to cut or chip with a knife}}, {{cog|sv|kuta}}, {{m|sv|kytti|t=a knife}}), {{cog|nb|kutte|t=to cut}}, {{cog|nn|kutte|t=to cut}}, {{cog|is|kuta|t=to cut with a knife}}, {{cog|non|kuti|t=small knife}}, {{cog|no|kyttel}}, {{m|no|kytel}}, {{m|no|kjutul|t=pointed slip of wood used to strip bark}}. {{displaced|enm|snithen}} (from {{m|ang|snīþan}}), still attested in dialectal {{m|en|snithe}} and {{m|en|snead}}. See {{m|en|snide}}.

The adjective sense of "drunk" (now rare and now usually used in the originally humorous derivative form of {{m|en|half-cut}}) dates from the 17th century, from {{m|en||cut in the leg}} or {{m|en||to have cut your leg}}, a {{lg|euphemism}} for being very drunk.

{{inh|en|gem-pro|*fastāną|t=to fast}}, from the same root as {{inh|en|gem-pro|*fastijaną|t=to fasten}}, derived from {{m|gem-pro|*fastuz}}, and thereby related to Etymology 1. The religious sense is presumably introduced in the Gothic church, from {{cog|got|𐍆𐌰𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌽||hold fast (viz. to the rule of abstinence)}}. This semantic development is unique to Gothic, the term glosses Greek {{m|grc|νηστεύω}}, Latin {{m|la|ieiuno}} which do not have similar connotations of "holding fast". The feminine noun {{cog|goh|fasta}} likely existed in the 8th century (shift to neuter {{cog|goh|fasten}} from the 9th century, whence modern {{cog|de|Fasten}}). The Old English noun originally had the sense "fortress, enclosure" and takes the religious sense only in late Old English, perhaps influenced by {{der|en|non|fasta}}. {{root|en|ine-pro|*sed-}}

{{senseno|en|site|uc=1}} (“location or site”) is probably derived from {{inh|en|ang|sǣte|t=house}}, which is related to {{cog|goh|sāza|t=sedan, seat, domicile}}.

##: {{ux|en|He sat on the arm of the chair rather than the '''seat''', which always annoyed his mother.}}
##: {{ux|en|the '''seat''' of a saddle}}
## {{senseid|en|sitting furniture}} A piece of furniture made for sitting, such as a [[chair]], [[stool]], or [[bench]]; any [[improvised]] place for sitting.

###: {{ux|en|Hey, fighter boy, our radar's putting out enough energy to launch your '''seat''' from this distance!}}

##: {{ux|en|Instead of saying "sit down", she said "place your '''seat''' on this chair".}}

##: {{ux|en|The '''seat''' of these trousers is almost worn through.}}

##: {{ux|en|Washington D.C. is the '''seat''' of the U.S. government.}}
